quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have never buy] anything from that online store before.
quests.hint: The present perfect needs 'have' plus the past participle, not the base verb.
quests.explanation: The present perfect requires the past participle after 'have': 'have never bought,' not 'have never buy.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Have you ever return] an item to this shop before?
quests.hint: The present perfect question needs the past participle, and the subject 'you' needs 'have.'
quests.explanation: Present perfect questions need 'Have' + subject + past participle: 'Have you ever returned,' not the base verb.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [has already try on] three different dresses today at the boutique.
quests.hint: The present perfect needs the past participle, not the base verb, after 'has.'
quests.explanation: 'Has' must be followed by the past participle: 'has already tried on,' not the base form 'try on.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have never tasting] such spicy food in my entire life!
quests.hint: The present perfect needs 'have' plus the past participle, not the -ing form.
quests.explanation: The present perfect requires the past participle: 'have never tasted,' not the -ing form 'tasting.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Has your brother ever cook] a full meal by himself before?
quests.hint: The present perfect question needs the past participle, with 'Has' matching a singular subject.
quests.explanation: Present perfect questions with a singular subject use 'Has' + past participle: 'Has...ever cooked.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [have already eat], so we don't need a table right now, thank you.
quests.hint: The present perfect needs the past participle form after 'have,' not the base verb or simple past form.
quests.explanation: 'Have' must be followed by the past participle 'eaten,' not the base form 'eat' or the simple past 'ate.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have lost] my phone yesterday, so now I need a brand new one.
quests.hint: The time word 'yesterday' shows exactly when the action happened, pointing to a finished past action.
quests.explanation: A specific past time word like 'yesterday' requires the simple past 'lost,' not the present perfect.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [lost] my phone, so I can't call anyone right now until I find it.
quests.hint: There's no specific past time mentioned, just a present result of a past action.
quests.explanation: Without a specific past time, the present perfect 'have lost' connects the past action to its present result.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [repaired] her laptop three times since she bought it last year.
quests.hint: The phrase 'since she bought it' shows a connection between the past and now, with repeated actions.
quests.explanation: 'Since' often signals the present perfect for repeated actions up to now: 'has repaired,' not the simple past.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have seen] the doctor last Tuesday for a regular check-up.
quests.hint: The specific time phrase 'last Tuesday' points to a finished action at a known time.
quests.explanation: A specific past time expression like 'last Tuesday' requires the simple past 'saw,' not the present perfect.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [never took] this medicine before, so I'm not sure how it will affect me.
quests.hint: There's no specific past time mentioned, just experience up to now.
quests.explanation: Without a specific time, the present perfect 'have never taken' describes experience up to the present moment.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: He [went] to the gym three times this week already, which is impressive.
quests.hint: The phrase 'this week' is an unfinished period that includes now.
quests.explanation: Unfinished time periods like 'this week' often pair with the present perfect: 'has gone,' not the simple past.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: You [have to] buy a ticket in advance; you can simply pay at the door.
quests.hint: Think about something that is not necessary, since there's an alternative option mentioned.
quests.explanation: 'Don't have to' shows something isn't necessary, fitting a situation with another option, not 'have to.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [don't have to] arrive early if we want good seats at the concert.
quests.hint: Think about something necessary in order to get a good result.
quests.explanation: 'Have to' expresses necessity for a good result, not 'don't have to,' which means it's optional.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [have to] finish her project before she can watch the new series.
quests.hint: The subject 'she' is singular; think about the matching form expressing necessity.
quests.explanation: With a singular subject, 'has to' expresses necessity, not 'have to,' which pairs with plural subjects.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: You [have to] shout; I can hear you perfectly well from here.
quests.hint: Think about something unnecessary because the situation is already fine.
quests.explanation: 'Don't have to' shows something is unnecessary, fitting a calm situation, not 'have to.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [don't have to] reply to this email by Friday, according to the request.
quests.hint: Think about a deadline that creates necessity.
quests.explanation: 'Have to' expresses necessity created by a deadline, not 'don't have to,' which means it's optional.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: He [have to] explain everything again because no one understood the first time.
quests.hint: The subject 'he' is singular; think about something necessary for him to do.
quests.explanation: Singular subjects pair with 'has to' to express necessity, not the plural form 'have to.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The neighbor [which] lives next door always waters our plants when we travel.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a person, used as the subject of the clause.
quests.explanation: 'Who' is used for people as the subject of a relative clause, not 'which,' which refers to things.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The app [who] I use every morning tracks my sleep and daily steps.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a thing, here an app, not a person.
quests.explanation: 'Which' is used for things or objects, such as an app, not 'who,' which is reserved for people.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: That's the family [who's] dog always barks at night in our neighborhood.
quests.hint: We need a possessive relative pronoun showing the dog belongs to the family, not the contraction of 'who is.'
quests.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession, while 'who's' is a contraction of 'who is' and doesn't fit here.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The teacher [which] taught me chemistry last year just retired from the school.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a person, used as the subject.
quests.explanation: 'Who' refers to people, here the teacher, not 'which,' which refers to things.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The textbook [who] we use in class is quite old and a little outdated.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a thing, here a textbook, not a person.
quests.explanation: 'Which' refers to objects or things, such as a textbook, not 'who,' which is for people.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: That's the student [who's] backpack was left in the classroom yesterday.
quests.hint: We need a possessive relative pronoun showing the backpack belongs to the student.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession, while 'who's' is a contraction of 'who is' and doesn't fit this meaning.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If I [will finish] the report on time, my manager will be very happy.
quests.hint: First conditional uses the simple present in the 'if' clause, not the future form.
quests.explanation: In first conditional sentences, the 'if' clause uses the simple present: 'If I finish,' not 'will finish.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If you send the email now, the client [receives] it before the meeting starts.
quests.hint: The main clause of a first conditional sentence uses 'will' plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: The result clause of a first conditional uses 'will' + base verb: 'will receive,' not just 'receives.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If we [will have] enough time, we'll review the budget again tomorrow.
quests.hint: First conditional uses the simple present in the 'if' clause, not 'will.'
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional always uses the simple present: 'have,' not 'will have.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If the weather [will be] nice tomorrow, we'll go hiking in the mountains.
quests.hint: Remember that first conditional 'if' clauses stay in the present tense.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional sentence takes the simple present: 'is,' not 'will be.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If we miss this flight, we [have] to wait six hours for the next one.
quests.hint: The result clause of a first conditional sentence uses 'will' plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: The main clause of a first conditional uses 'will' + base verb: 'will have to wait,' not just 'have.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If you [will forget] your passport at home, you won't be able to board.
quests.hint: The condition itself is expressed with a present-tense verb here.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional sentence requires the simple present: 'forget,' not 'will forget.'
